Keywords: bar chart, comparison, categories, magnitude, ranking few
When to Use: Comparing a single measure across a small number of named categories where magnitude/ranking matters
When NOT to Use: Not for parts of one whole (use part-to-whole); not once category count exceeds ~7-8 (use comparison-many)
Data Volume Threshold: Comfortably readable up to ~7-8 categories in a print-width figure; beyond that, category-label collision on the axis becomes the limiting factor before perceptual accuracy does
Accessibility Notes: distinguish by pattern-fill or direct value labels, not hue alone, for greyscale/colorblind safety
Static Fallback: value label at each bar end
Anti-Patterns: 3D bars (Tufte: adds a perspective-distorted third dimension that misrepresents the actual 2D magnitude, pure chartjunk); rainbow/spectral palette across categories with no ordinal meaning (implies a false ranking, Few)

Keywords: ranked bar, sorted bar, many categories, leaderboard
Secondary Options: Dot plot; small multiples if also faceted by a second variable
When to Use: Many named categories where the reader needs rank/magnitude at a glance, not just a couple values
When NOT to Use: Beyond roughly 30-40 categories in one static figure, print label legibility breaks down before the chart form itself does -- use a sorted table or a top-N-plus-other truncation
Data Volume Threshold: Ceiling is category-label legibility at a legible print point size within the figure's available height, not perceptual accuracy
Accessibility Notes: sort order is itself an accessibility aid -- rank order lets position carry the message instead of forcing the reader to scan for magnitude
Static Fallback: value labels at bar ends where space allows; omit and let gridlines carry precision when categories are dense
Anti-Patterns: unsorted (alphabetical) ordering when the message is about rank (forces the reader to perform the sort the chart should have done); pie chart at this category count (Cleveland & McGill's angle/area accuracy degrades further as slice count rises, and >8 slices is unreadable at any accuracy)

Data Type: parts summing to one meaningful total
Keywords: pie, donut, stacked bar, proportion, share, percentage
Best Chart Type: Stacked bar (single bar, segmented) or 100% stacked bar
Secondary Options: Pie chart, only if <=5 slices and a single snapshot (no cross-total comparison); treemap for hierarchical parts with many categories
When to Use: Reader needs to see how one total divides into a small number of named shares
When NOT to Use: Never pie beyond ~5 slices; never pie to compare shares across multiple totals/time periods (angle-to-angle comparison across separate pies is a task humans are measurably bad at -- use 100% stacked bars or a slope chart)
Data Volume Threshold: <=5-6 parts before switching to stacked bar or a plain table
Accessibility Notes: label each segment/slice directly with name and value -- never rely on a separate legend requiring colour-matching across the page
Static Fallback: each part labelled with name + value/percentage on or beside the segment
Anti-Patterns: pie chart beyond 5-6 slices (angle/area is the least accurate perceptual judgment per Cleveland & McGill 1984, error compounds with slice count); 3D pie (adds perspective distortion on top of an already-weak angle judgment -- the front slice reads larger than an equal-area back slice, documented chartjunk, Tufte); comparing two or more pies to show change over time

Keywords: line chart, trend, trajectory, time series few
Secondary Options: Area chart, single series only (cumulative/volume) -- not stacked multi-series, which reintroduces part-to-whole's accuracy problem for the upper bands
When to Use: Showing a trend/trajectory over a continuous time axis for a small number of named series
When NOT to Use: Not for <=2 discrete time points -- a line implies continuous interpolation between points that don't exist; use a bar or slope chart for a simple before/after instead
Data Volume Threshold: <=3-4 lines before individual lines become hard to trace by eye in print -- lower than report 03's 5-7 spaghetti-chart ceiling on purpose, because print has no hover-to-isolate a line
A11y Fallback: data table of key time points
Accessibility Notes: differentiate lines by colour AND line style/dash, never colour alone, so greyscale photocopies stay distinguishable
Static Fallback: each line labelled with its series name at its terminal point
Anti-Patterns: dual y-axes (Few: pairing two independently-scaled series on a shared x-axis implies a visual correlation between their slopes that is an artifact of arbitrary axis scaling, not a real relationship -- one of the most-cited misleading-chart patterns); smoothing/trend curves without showing the underlying data points (hides real variance, a Tufte data-integrity concern)

Keywords: small multiples, spaghetti chart, many series over time
Best Chart Type: Small multiples (one mini-chart per series, shared axis scale)
Secondary Options: Sorted line highlighting only the top N with the rest greyed as context; heatmap/strip chart if series count is very high and only relative pattern matters
When to Use: Many series need to be shown and the point is comparing shape/pattern across them, not reading exact values off one crowded chart
When NOT to Use: Never as a single overlaid multi-line chart beyond report 03's 5-7 spaghetti threshold -- the fix is small multiples, not a bigger legend
Data Volume Threshold: >4-5 series triggers this form instead of the few-series line chart; small multiples scale to dozens of panels as long as each panel stays legible at its allotted size -- a page-layout constraint from T7, not a perceptual one
A11y Fallback: data table, or a ranked summary table of top/bottom N series by one summary statistic
Accessibility Notes: consistent y-axis scale across all panels is what makes shape genuinely comparable -- variable per-panel scales silently misrepresent relative magnitude, Tufte's lie-factor concern applied to small multiples
Static Fallback: n/a -- small multiples are inherently the static-safe form; each panel titled with its series name, no shared legend needed
Print Series Max: n/a -- bounded by page layout (T7), not a perceptual limit
Anti-Patterns: single overlaid chart with >5-7 lines (report 03 Section B's spaghetti-chart threshold -- worse in print than on screen, since there is no hover-to-isolate a line); inconsistent y-axis scale across small-multiple panels (defeats the entire purpose of the form -- shape comparisons become meaningless, Tufte)

Data Type: one or few continuous variables, shape/spread matters
Keywords: histogram, box plot, distribution, spread, outliers
Best Chart Type: Histogram (single variable) or box plot (comparing distribution across a few groups)
Secondary Options: Dot/strip plot for small n; violin plot only for a statistically literate audience
When to Use: The message is about spread/shape/outliers within a variable, not a single summary number
When NOT to Use: Don't present binned bar counts as a histogram without stating bin width -- bin width materially changes the shape shown, and an undisclosed choice misrepresents the data
Data Volume Threshold: Box plots compare cleanly across <=8-10 groups in print before group labels no longer fit legibly; beyond that, small multiples of histograms
A11y Fallback: summary statistics table (mean, median, quartiles, min/max)
Accessibility Notes: always state the bin width on a histogram directly in the caption -- a data-integrity disclosure, not decoration
Static Fallback: n/a -- static-native form; box-plot groups labelled below each box
Caption Must State: must state bin width for histograms specifically
Anti-Patterns: unlabeled bin width on a histogram (the most common way a distribution chart silently misrepresents its data -- the same dataset can look unimodal or bimodal purely from bin-width choice, Tufte); violin plot for a general/non-technical audience without explanation (asks the reader to decode a compound density shape most readers were never taught -- a box plot conveys the same core information at lower chart-literacy cost)

Data Type: two continuous variables, relationship between them
Keywords: scatter plot, correlation, relationship, trend line
Secondary Options: Connected scatter, only if a third ordering variable like time matters too; scatter matrix for more than 2 variables
When to Use: Showing whether/how two continuous measures relate
When NOT to Use: Don't imply causation the data doesn't support -- state 'correlation, not causation' in the caption where readers are likely to over-infer
Data Volume Threshold: Print-legible up to a few hundred points before overplotting hides individual points; beyond that use a density/hexbin form or a summary trend line with a stated sample size
A11y Fallback: correlation coefficient stated in the caption/text, plus the underlying data table if small enough
Accessibility Notes: if overplotting exists in the source data, disclose it -- don't quietly thin the data without saying so
Caption Must State: should state sample size (n) and, where relevant, the correlation coefficient
Anti-Patterns: trend line shown without the underlying scatter points (hides the actual data density/outliers the reader needs to judge how much to trust the line, Tufte); implying causation in the caption/surrounding text for a chart form that can only show correlation

Data Type: ordered categorical, rank/order itself is the message
Keywords: ranking, leaderboard, slope chart, bump chart, rank change
Secondary Options: Slope chart / bump chart, specifically when rank change over two or more time points is the message
When to Use: The reader's task is 'who is first, who is last, who moved' rather than 'what is the exact value'
When NOT to Use: Don't use a slope/bump chart beyond ~8-10 ranked items -- crossing lines become illegible at that density, the same crowding mechanism as change-over-time-many
Data Volume Threshold: Sorted bar ranks up to ~20-30 items in print with a top/bottom-N-plus-truncation note; slope charts cap lower, ~8-10, per above
Accessibility Notes: print explicit rank numbers (1, 2, 3...) next to each item -- removes any ambiguity sorted position alone might leave, especially in greyscale
Static Fallback: explicit rank number as a direct label, not position alone
Anti-Patterns: unsorted bars when rank is the stated message (forces the reader to perform the sort the chart should have done); rainbow palette across ranked items with no other categorical meaning (implies a second dimension of meaning the colour doesn't actually carry, Few)

Data Type: values tied to named geographic regions
Best Chart Type: Choropleth map (single measure across defined regions)
Secondary Options: Proportional symbol map when regions vary hugely in area; a sorted bar chart of the same regions is very often the better print choice
When to Use: Only when the geographic pattern itself (clustering, regional spread) is the message, not merely because the data has a region column
When NOT to Use: Don't default to a map just because the data has a region label -- if the task is 'which region is highest,' a sorted bar answers it more accurately and more compactly (choropleth relies on area/colour-value judgment, one of Cleveland & McGill's weakest perceptual tasks; a bar's length is one of the strongest)
Data Volume Threshold: Legibility caps at the point where individual regions can no longer be resolved at the page's print size/DPI -- small/dense regions (e.g. small European countries at page-width scale) often fall below that floor and need an inset
Accessibility Notes: never rely on a colour ramp alone -- direct-label the highest/lowest few regions with their value, and always ship the underlying table for readers who cannot resolve a colour-value legend
Static Fallback: n/a -- static-native form; the data table alongside it is the real fallback for readers who cannot parse the ramp
Anti-Patterns: multi-hue rainbow ramp for a sequential (low-to-high) value scale (implies false categorical breaks in a continuous scale, and is the least colourblind-safe/greyscale-safe encoding in this table -- a single-hue lightness ramp reads correctly in every reproduction condition a multi-hue ramp fails); 3D relief/extrusion map styling (a fake third dimension on top of the weakest perceptual task in the table, compounding area/colour judgment with occlusion)

Data Type: sequential steps, transitions, or quantity flowing between named stages
Keywords: flowchart, process diagram, sankey, sequence, workflow
Secondary Options: Sankey diagram specifically when flow quantity between stages is the message; plain numbered list with connecting arrows for a strictly linear, non-branching process
When to Use: Reader needs to understand order/sequence/branching logic, or (Sankey) proportional flow quantities between stages
When NOT to Use: Don't use a Sankey beyond ~5-6 stages/nodes -- crossing flow-bands become as unreadable as an overplotted line chart; don't use a flowchart's branching vocabulary for a strictly linear list with no decisions
Data Volume Threshold: Flowcharts stay legible up to ~10-15 steps/nodes on a print page before needing a fold-out or multi-page spread; Sankeys cap much lower, ~5-6 stages
A11y Fallback: numbered/ordered text list of steps, or a from-to table of flow quantities for a Sankey
Accessibility Notes: arrows must be unambiguous even with colour stripped (photocopy) -- use arrowheads and directional layout (top-to-bottom or left-to-right), never colour alone for direction
Static Fallback: n/a -- static-native form; every step/node labelled in place, no legend needed for a well-drawn flowchart
Print Series Max: n/a -- ceiling is stage/node count (see Data Volume Threshold), not a series count
Anti-Patterns: more than ~5-6 nodes in a Sankey diagram (crossing flow-bands become as unreadable as an overplotted line chart -- the same crowding mechanism as report 03's spaghetti-chart threshold, applied to area instead of line); decorative 3D/bevelled flowchart boxes (Tufte chartjunk -- adds visual weight with zero information content, competing with the arrows and labels that actually carry the message)

Data Type: precise individual values the reader needs to reference, not a pattern to perceive at a glance
Keywords: table, lookup, reference, exact values, pricing sheet
Best Chart Type: Table (no chart -- this row's point is that the right answer is explicitly 'no chart')
When to Use: Report 03 Section B's own rule, restated as this row's defining criterion: use a table when the audience needs to read/reference exact individual values (e.g. a pricing sheet)
When NOT to Use: Don't use a table when the reader's actual task is comparing magnitude or spotting a trend -- that's the flip side of the same report 03 rule, and a bar or line chart serves it better
Data Volume Threshold: n/a -- tables scale with page length/multi-page spreads, governed by report 03 Section D's own table-design rules, not a row/column ceiling
A11y Fallback: n/a -- a table IS the fallback form for every other row in this file
Accessibility Notes: report 03 Section D's table rules apply directly: tabular (fixed-width) figures for numeric columns, right-align numbers/left-align text, minimal vertical rules, sparse horizontal rules (header + total only); grade rationale: a table is the ground-truth data, no perceptual-encoding step to fail at
Print Palette Roles: n/a -- zebra striping is a screen-allowed, print-discouraged pattern per report 03/research 06; this row's point is that no chart palette applies
Caption Must State: and captioned ABOVE the table, not below, per report 03 Section D and T10's Caption Position convention
Anti-Patterns: forcing a chart where a table was the right answer, specifically to look more 'designed' -- Few's core argument and the single most common chart-selection mistake in business documents: a bar chart of 4 numbers a reader needed to look up precisely is strictly worse than just printing the 4 numbers
